I'm digging through some text files that I kept some notes on and I found some stuff that may be useful if you like to write bash scripts.

 #!/bin/bash

 # Absolute value
 abs() {
 [ $1 -lt 0 ] && echo $((-$1)) || echo $1
 }

 # Greatest Common Divsior
 gcd() {
 local a=$(abs $1)
 local b=$(abs $2)
 while [ $a -ne $b ]; do
 [ $a -gt $b ] && a=$(( $a - $b )) || b=$(( $b - $a ))
 done
 echo $a
 }

 # Lowest Common Multiple
 lcm() {
 local g=$(gcd $1 $2)
 local p=$(($1 * $2))
 p=$(abs $p)
 echo $(( $p / $g ))
 }

For more floating point functionality, it's generally recommended to use awk, or a high level language that has math support.

Bash is good for integer math, but not so good with floating points. The bc (bash calculator) is proof of that.

 pi=$(echo "4*a(1)" | bc -l) # Returns the value of pi, but the last digit is wrong

Bash will save pi as 3.14159265358979323844. The true value of pi to 20 digits 3.14159265358979323846 according to Wolfram Alpha. (Wolfram queries this as pi to 21 digits.)

What if we're not that picky? Surely 10 digits is good enough for anyone right?

 pi=$(echo "scale=10; 4*a(1)" | bc -l) # Returns the value of pi to 10 digits, but the last digit is wrong

Nope. Instead we get 3.1415926532. The true value of pi to 10 digits 3.1415926536 according to Wolfram Alpha. (Wolfram queries this as pi to 11 digits.

So because bc is bad ad floating point, bash can't be use for complex math.

You could try using awk. However you'll need to pass input to awk otherwise it will run endlessly.

 awk '{ print 4*atan2(1,1); }' # You will go nowhere. Better CTRL+C to call off this operation.
 ^C

 pi=$(echo "1" | awk '{ print $1 *4*atan2(1,1); }') # This works but it's much longer
 3.14159 # Good but lacks scale.

 pi=$(echo "1" | awk '{ printf "%0.10f\n", $1*4*atan2(1,1); }') # adding "\n" is optional, but the formatting necessary 
 3.1415926536 # Perfect!

We could use this to make bc-style math commands using awk and encapsulated in bash functions. Maybe I'll share that later.
